I adore this game, it's a very unique RPG. It's familiar JRPG turn-based combat but rather than fighting with a small party of 4 characters you can recruit over 40 units and arrange them into battalions. Your battalions will then move around the battlefield individually and take general orders from you like you're the commander of the an army. Despite fighting on a bigger scale, they still make the individual units that you recruit interesting and likeable with their own questions and personalities.

I also love a lot of the games design - the character models can be a bit iffy but the locations are gorgeous even after 15 years, and the monster designs are incredible. Even though the game's story is fairly standard JRPG-spiel, I really like the world they created with all the different races, politics and mysterious remnant creatures that nobody seems to understand.

HOWEVER! Despite playing this game through several times to completion, I don't think I could recommend it to anyone else. There are so many little design flaws that get on your nerves, for example:
[list][*] For some reason the game only gives you access to really basic skills for the first half of the game, then you start unlocking all the cool unique spells right near the end. It takes a really long time to level up your skills so it just doesn't feel worth it to start levelling something new when you're most of the way through the game. Even when I did a 100% completion run there were several different skill types that I just never explored because it wasn't worth it.

[*] You give your battalions general commands and the individual units within them will decide based on that which ability to use in combat. Early game I really wanted to level up some of my unit's magic skill but they would only use it like 10% of the time so it was agony and I ended up just dropping them for units later who already came with strong magic. Later in the game a unit choosing one ability over the other can make a huge difference in a fight. 

[*] Similar to the above point, the game only generates 5 possible commands you can pick from each turn (for each battalion). Sometimes the one you really want just isn't listed. Several times I lost a difficult boss battle because my battalion with several healers in it just didn't generate the "Heal Yourself" command despite being near death. You might want to use your super powerful Omnistrike skill against a particular enemy, but for some reason the option only generated for a different enemy. Etc.

[*] There are hundreds of side quests in the game if you enjoy 100%ing, but many of them are just pure torture. E.g. there are lots of quests to kill bosses that spawn rarely within a particular location. So you might have to pick a location, load in, run for several minutes through the location to get to the area where the boss might spawn, and if it didn't you run all the way out again and repeat. A lot of the bosses I found relatively easily, but some of them genuinely took me HOURS. So for hours I am not playing the game, I'm just running in and out of a dungeon a hundred times. There are also lots of quests to farm particular materials from a particular enemy, and that can be similar. Run into a dungeon to the exact location this type of enemy spawns, though sometimes it doesn't. Kill that enemy for a 5% chance to get the material, if not run all the way out and back in again. Oh and you need to get 3 to complete the quest... Sometimes I would be killing a Demon to get a Demon Tooth for a quest, and it wouldn't drop for hours. Only to look it up on the Wiki and it turns out that for some reason only the Demons in one particular location drop that material, not the exact same Demons in a different location. WHY

[*] As above, so much information is not given to you in the game - you need to refer to the wiki. How to change a units class, how to unlock high level formations for your battalions (gives them a huge buff), how to learn the strongest magic, how to find rare enemies. You spend about as much time reading the wiki as you do playing the game.

[*] Managing your units can be a pain. You don't manage their equipment directly, they just constantly ask you to give them materials so they can upgrade themselves. When you have 40 units in your army the popups are endless. Often they will be asking for a material you can't even get right now because it's locked behind 2 hours of side quests. And you can't give them materials you already have for some reason - If a unit starts asking for Iron Ore, and you already have 20 of them in your inventory, you will still need to go out and gather the extra ore for them and can't just hand them what you already have. If you find a cool accessory units will randomly start asking for it, but you can't control who. So you might want to give it to a particular unit but they never ask you for it and other units ask you for it 500 times and never stop no matter how many times you say no. There's no "No, and don't ask again" option.

In my opinion this game was a flawed masterpiece, that with some tweaks or a sequel could have been amazing. The battle system is super-interesting, innovative, and fun, even though it has several problems if/when you actually discover the inner workings (e.g. some possibilities of abuse like disengaging and criss-crossing units each round if you are faster, and also other interesting options that don't ever actually work as designed, e.g. the option to use long range attacks is very rarely useful because you can't actually maintain distance from enemies, although in later fights you may *begin* more distant). 
The fact that you cannot choose each specific input but only give slightly general commands to a unit actually makes sense from a gameplay design perspectvie (it would take forever for each battle otherwise) but also makes it fun and realistic in a sense, it gives the impressions that you are a battlefield commander, not some sort of hive-mind, and each unit will indeed follow your orders but deciding the details by themselves. However, although very infrequent, it does happen at times that you do not receive any command choice that you like for a given situation. Also, some skills are so strong that many fights can be trivialized if you discover the specific conditions needed to trigger them.
Given it was an innovative system, it had huge potential for a series IMO. Sadly, this game was not successful and will never get a sequel, what a shame.
Also, the rpg mechanisms have an incredible number of options to go for (almost limitless combinations of classes and skills), although, for some mysterious reasons, the game does NOT explain basically ANYTHING to you and you don't get to intentionally choose anything, everything you get good at depends on what you are actually using in battle (remember to turn off skills you don't want to use).
In fact, the main plot (though for once fairly interesting) is like 5% of the game, the rest is side quests, secret bosses, and secret weapons hunting, and you literally cannot truly experience the game without a guide, which is baffling.

Going into this game I was hoping to find a classic JRPG made by sqeenix, with the acceptable grind, lovely characters and an enjoyable time. Well I got anything but that last part.

The maing gripe I have with the game is the difficult combat system paired with the penalizing Battle Rank (BR) system. The combat is nice once you get the hang of it, though I find it very confusing that the only way to learn the combat normally; trying to get into as many fights as you can, is penalized heavily by the BR system.

The BR system is not your level, but it's a rank that goes up according to the amount of fights you've had, the higher it gets the more difficult the enemies get. Not so bad right? Well if you manage to somehow get your BR high before a section of the game played in Nest of Eagles you may very well get stuck here, this only being the first half of the game leads you to redo the entire game up to that point, mostlikely following a guide telling you to keep your BR low. (Not what happened in my case, but I was close to doing this)

Not only does the BR system make the fights harder it also makes powering up the later characters you get in part 2 harder to make useful. Now this happened to me. The workaround being farming a unique monster called Bai Ze or in this releases case you could also opt to farm insects at the cost of two unique units. This allows you to farm your characters up to an acceptable stat range or to help you in cheesing the game.

The combat is done in unions; groups of characters in formations, different formations give different stat bonuses. The unions then have "random" actions that they can do. Herein lies the problem, the actions I want to do are the actions that, most of the time, are not readily available while I feel this takes away from the strategic point of view, it enforces defensive play and working with what you have; it does however make the difficulty of the strategy feel articficial since instead of giving a difinitive way to take on a fight, you have to hope you get those actions to pop-up.

The problem comes from the combat and penalizing BR system, you try to learn the game and do all the sidequests once they're all available, raising your BR to a level the game didn't expect you to have and making the rest of the fights too difficult to progress. The sidequests may be optional but some of them become too much to handle, the solutions being to farm a unique monster, to spam hard to trigger arcana spells, and to change your formation into one that simply bumrushes the boss and hope that they die before you get killed. If you still think the game is a fair challenge after this go ahead and buy it, I know it's old but for a game to be unforgiving to a point where you cannot progress the story is just wrong.

The story was meh, I felt it was a little confusing at times, and not particularly gripping. The battle mechanics were what really drew me in. It's brilliant! I've put in way more hours than the recorded 15. Once you run through the game fully, you get to start a new game in hard mode which is a whole other challenge (worth the torture, in my opinion).

As plenty of people below have pointed out, combat is turn-based and rather than controlling single characters, you can fight with 'unions' of characters. At each turn, you give general commands to each of the unions, and the AI picks the different attacks/spells for each of the union members (you can see what gets picked, but you can't change this specifically during battle). And that's one fun part of the battle system- it might seem like all their actions are out of your control, but careful union setup with suitably trained characters makes a HUGE difference in the sets of commands you get. You even get to fine tune the kinds of attack/spells each union member can execute by blocking some of their learned skills. This helps increase the chances of the AI picking up the attacks you want, since you've removed the ones you didn't need, even if it's just for a particular battle.

You're free to set up your unions as you wish- have separate unions for offense/tanking/healing/debuffing (like most sane people), just have an army of attackers slashing through monsters (this may actually end badly...), maybe, like I usually prefer, have self-contained unions capable of looking after themselves in battle so that you can forgo a healing union altogether, or all of these at different points in the game. You'll need a bit of care with how the unions are set up and how members are trained, otherwise the commands generated during battle can be really useless and frustrating. There's a lot of flexibility to this system, which becomes clearer as you progress further into the game and begin handling more unions; if you've trained your characters decently enough in their roles(warrior/thaumaturge/mage/warrior-mage/whatnot), you can swap them around a lot and calibrate their skills to try different kinds of union set-ups, and this allows you to try out any number of strategies for tough battles. That said, there will always be few hiccups out of your hand. Veeery few, if the unions are decent. 

The other fun part about the battle system is that once you've worked out a few stable union combinations, just hit the spacebar and the AI does all the gritty work really well, and you can focus on your overall battle strategy/approach instead.

Stat increases are not random, their general direction of growth will depend on how you use the characters. Spam spells all the time and you'll see your characters' INT levelling far quicker that STR, and finally ending at a much higher number. But this is as far as our immediate control over stats gets, as far as I'm aware.

There is a 'morale bar' on every battle screen, and the gauge changes depending on how the battle's going. Maintining a decent morale in your favour can have a big impact in boss fights especially.

The game does have a strange levelling system, where grinding is not always rewarded (there are a couple of tricks to super-powering your characters early on at specific spots in the game via grinding, but that just really sucks the fun out of the whole experience). This, I feel, is a good thing; gives you more time to just explore the world, kill all the monsters, loot all the dungeons. Contrary to what's mentioned often, you don't have to skip -all- battles at first or be excessively wary about over-levelling. I have a habit of clearing out every new map, which is just what I did for my first playthrough, and ended the game at a Battle Rank of 144. Some of the boss battles were hard, but not too hard (except the Lost Remnant, maybe), and certainly not unbeatable. The hardest point in the main storyline in that playthrough was the part called 'The Nest of Eagles'- took 4 tries to finish it at ~BR 60 (considered a fairly high BR by most for this part of the game), but the fight needed a whole lot of re-organising on my part, and this made the win even more satisfying. Basically, the higher your Battle Rank, the more challenging the fights can get, but they rarely become insurmountable. I personally love the lack of intense grinding here, it just let me play the game to the end casually the first time around.

There are several classes you can train each of your characters to get into, depending on what skill sets they can acquire, and which ones you focus on. The Wiki is a great place for all the information you need on classes (and everything else). There are lots of weapons to choose from (a plus for me), each with different upgrade paths. Lots of scope for crafting. Nice loot from the bosses.  With the game config files as is, however, you can only change your main character's equipment. The others have set weapon paths, and you can only choose their upgrade focus (combat/mystic/balance).

There are lots of sidequests to complete; the bulk of your time will probably be spent on these. So if you become friends with the battle system, this can only be a good thing. 

The DLC battles are great, in my view. My favourite part of the playthrough.

Graphics are cool, but this point is probably very subjective. 

I've had no issues running this game, performance-wise (on a system with recommended specs), and have been able to run this on a system with specs slightly lower than the minimum suggested (significant lag, but that's where I finished my first 3-odd playthroughs, and I loved the gameplay enough for this to not trouble me!)

If there's one major complaint I have, it's that far too many playable characters come too late into the game, and are much weaker than your current set of characters. If you don't watch the BR, this difference becomes even more stark. 
Or sometimes they're really cool, but you're almost at the end of the game so what's the point in hiring them.

TLDR; the battle system is very intriguing, give it a shot! Especially if you like battles. The game seems to be perpetually discounted on here anyway.
